passage.title: The Machine That Learned to Translate
paragraphs: In 1954, a computer at Georgetown University translated sixty Russian sentences into English. The scientists announced that translation would be solved in three or four years. They were wrong by about half a century.

The first systems worked with rules: somebody had to write down the grammar of both languages, word by word. The results were famous for being funny rather than useful. Everything changed when engineers stopped teaching computers grammar and started showing them examples instead. A modern system has read millions of pages that human translators had already translated, and it copies the patterns it finds.

Today a free application on your phone can translate a menu or an email in less than a second. Professional translators use these tools every day, and most of them say the same thing: the machine gives you a first draft, and then the real work begins.

The problem is that a language is not only a system of words. A joke, a legal contract and a poem all need somebody who understands who is speaking, to whom, and why. A machine can produce a correct sentence; whether it produces the right one is a different question.

It translated sixty Russian sentences into English.
It read millions of pages of translation.

passage.title: The Voice in the Kitchen
paragraphs: On November 2, 1920, a station in Pittsburgh broadcast the results of an American presidential election. Almost nobody heard it: there were perhaps a thousand receivers in the whole country. Ten years later, radio was in half the homes of the United States, and families had started to arrange their furniture around it.

Radio did something no newspaper had ever been able to do. It arrived at the same second in every house, and it did not ask the listener to know how to read. Governments understood this very quickly, and so did advertisers.

Television was supposed to kill it. It didn't. Radio moved into the car, and later into the kitchen and the workshop, because it is the only medium you can follow while your hands and your eyes are busy doing something else.

Today more people listen to spoken audio than at any moment in history, although most of them call it a podcast. Whatever we call it, the format has not changed much: one voice, talking to one person who is doing something else.

items.stem: Why did radio survive television?
choices: Because you can follow it while your hands and eyes are busy.
